result:
At dawn the city is still negotiating with itself. The streetlights go out one by one, reluctantly, as if admitting defeat to a sun that has not yet warmed the pavement. Buses drag their sighing bodies through intersections. A baker opens his shutters and releases the first honest scent of the day—yeast, sugar, browned crust, the smell of tomorrow being prepared before most people have decided to participate in it.

I like this hour because everything seems possible and nothing has been wasted yet. The headline has not arrived. The argument has not been sent. The errand may still be postponed. Even the pigeons look briefly philosophical, fluffed against the gray, considering the rooftops as if rooftops were ideas.

Somewhere a dog announces the arrival of a leaf. Somewhere a nurse checks her phone before an early shift. Somewhere a student who stayed up too long slides into a desk and pretends attention. Morning is not innocent exactly; it is generous. It hands everyone the same small collection of minutes and lets us decide whether to spend them quarreling, hurrying, noticing, or making toast.

Eventually the light strengthens, and the city becomes louder, brighter, less mysterious. But for a little while, if you are awake early enough, you can catch the world before it fully put on its costume of certainty. You can see the wires, the scaffolding, the cats, the quiet timers in kitchens counting toward breakfast.

Then the day begins in earnest, and we forget the brief truce of morning. Still, it waits tomorrow, patient as bread rising.
